::: {#play .lx-sec}
```{=html}
<div class="lx-interactive" data-learn="systems-map" data-src="../assets/learn/data/f02-systems-and-map.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The lab's three stations, in brief</p>
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>A reservoir</dt><dd>Holding up to 350 GWh and fed by a river averaging 101 MW, it gets through the year without spilling or running dry only with a steady release from 100 to 115 MW (the slider moves in 5 MW steps).</dd>
<dt>A battery</dt><dd>A 25 MW, 100 MWh battery that loses 20% on charging must buy 125 MWh to deliver 100.</dd>
<dt>A carbon budget</dt><dd>If Prairieland halves its 100 Mt a year by 2035 and holds there, its cumulative emissions still rise, from 825 Mt to 2,575 Mt by 2070, past a 1,500 Mt budget.</dd>
<dt>Feedback loops</dt><dd>More EVs bring more chargers, which bring more EVs: a reinforcing loop. Longer queues at chargers slow the growth, and the rebound effect takes back part of an efficiency saving: balancing loops.</dd>
<dt>The system map</dt><dd>Each of four levers reaches technology, cost, emissions, people and security within three waves.</dd>
</dl>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f2-fbt">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Lever</th><th scope="col">First wave</th><th scope="col">Later waves</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Gas price doubles</td><td>Wholesale price rises; gas heating costs more; the gas import bill rises</td><td>Plant mix shifts; CO₂ depends on what replaces gas; energy burden rises; investment shifts and dependence on imported gas falls</td></tr>
<tr><td>A heat wave</td><td>Demand rises; lines carry less; spare capacity falls; heat-related health risk rises</td><td>Prices and CO₂ can rise; bills and burden can rise later; tight hours can encourage new capacity</td></tr>
<tr><td>A carbon price</td><td>Gas plants can move ahead of coal plants; wholesale price rises</td><td>If gas replaces coal, CO₂ and local pollution fall; bills rise if the tariff passes the price on; the burden depends on the revenue; jobs shift</td></tr>
<tr><td>A new data center</td><td>Demand rises; it needs new connections; spare capacity falls when it connects; jobs and tax base can rise; cooling water depends on the design</td><td>CO₂ depends on what serves it; who pays for upgrades depends on the tariff; new supply may follow</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you run these yourself: three tanks, two loops and four levers.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Tanks:</b> the reservoir, lesson 9's battery and Prairieland's budget are illustrative.<br><b>Units:</b> Mt = million tonnes; GWh = a thousand MWh.<br><b>Map:</b> first-round directions of change, other things equal, for a grid like the Plains Grid; it states no sizes.<br><b>Waves:</b> steps in tracing causes; each label says roughly when a step plays out.<br><b>Data center:</b> an illustrative 300 MW load.</span></p>
```
:::

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f2-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Stock</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="stock">stock</span> is an amount that builds up or drains: water, stored energy, cumulative CO₂, cars on the road.</dd>
<dt>Flow</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="flow">flow</span> is a rate that fills or drains a stock; only flows change a stock.</dd>
<dt>Reinforcing loop</dt><dd>An even number of − links round a <span class="lx-term" data-term="feedback-loop">feedback loop</span>: change feeds itself (<span class="lx-term" data-term="reinforcing-loop">reinforcing</span>).</dd>
<dt>Balancing loop</dt><dd>An odd number of − links: the loop opposes the change that started it (<span class="lx-term" data-term="balancing-loop">balancing</span>); with long delays it can overshoot.</dd>
<dt>Ripple</dt><dd>One change spreads step by step across technology, cost, emissions, people and security: some effects at once, some years later.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The stocks that shape energy systems</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Many slow, hard questions are questions about stocks.

- **Equipment.** Power plants, buildings, cars and boilers last for decades, so today's choices stay in the stock long after: new purchases are the inflow, retirements the outflow. National pathways track this (Analyst lesson A20, Modeler lesson M13, upcoming).
- **Fuel.** Gas in storage and emergency oil stocks buffer a supply shock (Analyst lesson A21, upcoming).
- **Stored energy.** Reservoirs and batteries move energy in time ([lesson 9](09-storage.html); Analyst lesson A8, upcoming).
- **Cumulative CO₂ emissions.** Warming tracks them: the IPCC's best estimate is 0.45 °C for each 1,000 Gt of CO₂ (Gt = billion tonnes; likely 0.27 to 0.63 °C).
- **Net zero.** Stabilising human-induced warming requires [net zero]{.lx-term term="net-zero"} CO₂. The lab's counter records emissions only; land and oceans absorb part, so the CO₂ left in the air is a different stock.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From diagrams to equations</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A stock is a state variable that carries over from one step to the next:

$$
S_{t+1} = S_t + \big(\mathit{in}_t - \mathit{out}_t\big)\,\Delta t, \qquad 0 \le S_t \le \bar{S}
$$

with $S_t$ the stock, $\mathit{in}_t$ and $\mathit{out}_t$ the flows, $\Delta t$ the step and $\bar{S}$ the ceiling. Flow × time must come out in the stock's unit:

- **Reservoir:** change in GWh = (river in − release, in MW) × 168 hours ÷ 1,000, since 1 GWh = 1,000 MWh.
- **Carbon:** change in Mt = emissions in Mt a year × 1 year.
- **Battery:** the rule of [lesson 9](09-storage.html), with an efficiency on the inflow.

A loop appears when a flow depends on a stock, such as sales that depend on the EVs already on the road.

- **Simulation** steps such rules forward from given decisions; system dynamics, one method family in [R3](r03-system-and-method.html), writes the loops as equations.
- **Optimization** chooses the decisions ([lessons 10 to 13](10-write-it-down.html)).
- Which one a study needs is Researcher lesson R3.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lab leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Sizes: the map shows directions, not how much. Sizes need a model with data, prices and rules (Analyst and Modeler tiers).</li>
<li>Place and time: the same lever plays out differently in another region, market or year.</li>
<li>Many more links: a real system has far more parts and loops than fifteen cards and two diagrams.</li>
<li>Who decides: each ripple crosses the scales of <a href="f01-five-scales.html">F1</a>, and trade-offs between goals are Analyst lesson <a href="a22-tradeoff-explorer.html">A22</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: four myths, then five questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f2-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="inflow" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the inflow to a stock is falling, the stock is falling.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A stock falls only when its outflow exceeds its inflow. In one test, business-school students new to these ideas showed a poor grasp of stocks and flows (Booth Sweeney and Sterman, 2000).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="steady" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Holding CO₂ emissions steady holds the warming they cause steady.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Warming tracks cumulative CO₂ emissions, a stock: steady emissions keep adding to it. The IPCC finds net zero CO₂ is required to stabilise human-induced warming.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="growth" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A reinforcing loop always means growth.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It reinforces whichever way it turns: fewer EVs, fewer chargers built, fewer EVs.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rebound" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If people use a more efficient appliance more, the efficiency gain is wasted.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth: one review concludes that the direct rebound for household energy services in OECD (mostly high-income) countries should generally be less than 30%, so most of the saving is kept (Sorrell et al., 2009).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f2">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="stocklimit" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Prairie Town's battery is rated 25 MW and 100 MWh. Which number limits the stock?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">25 MW</li><li data-value="b">100 MWh</li><li data-value="c">Both equally</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>100 MWh is the stock it can hold; 25 MW limits the flow in or out. Together: 4 hours at full power.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="solarloop" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">More rooftop solar → lower midday prices → less income per new panel → less new rooftop solar. Which kind of loop?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Reinforcing</li><li data-value="b">Balancing</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Balancing: one − link (more solar, lower prices), so the loop pushes back on its own growth.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="heat" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Why does a heat wave squeeze spare capacity from both sides?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Demand rises while hot lines and some thermal plants deliver less</li><li data-value="b">Prices rise, so plants sell less</li><li data-value="c">Solar stops at noon</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Demand rises for cooling while hot lines sag and carry less and some thermal plants lose output: both sides of the balance move against the grid.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wave2" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A 300 MW data center connects, and no new supply comes with it. When does spare capacity shrink?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Years later, after a second event</li><li data-value="b">At once, as soon as the load connects</li><li data-value="c">Never: demand and supply are separate</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>At once: the extra demand uses up spare capacity when it connects. The map's waves trace causes in order; they are not always apart in time.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sizes" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">The map says bills “rise” after a carbon price. What would you need to say by how much?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">More arrows on the map</li><li data-value="b">A survey of opinions</li><li data-value="c">A model with data: plants, fuel prices, the carbon price and the tariff</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A model with data. The map shows directions; sizes come from models like the ones the Analyst and Modeler tiers build.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<li><b>Sized with data:</b> real studies measure how strong such loops are; the lab only shows their shape.</li>
